extras.markdown:
# How to use this guide

Pharmacognosy is a memory subject: botanical names, families, constituents, uses and tests. Short daily revision works far better than one long session. Study one chapter at a time, read the notes, cover them and write the monograph headings from memory, then answer the question bank without looking.

## Exam pattern (HPTSB, ER-2020)

The D.Pharm first-year theory paper is a yearly (annual) examination conducted by the board under the PCI Education Regulations 2020.

| Part | Marks |
| --- | --- |
| Board (university) theory examination | 80 marks, 3 hours |
| Sessional (internal) assessment by the college | 20 marks |
| **Total for ER20-13T** | **100 marks** |

The practical (ER20-13P) is assessed separately in the same way (board practical examination plus sessional marks).

**Paper pattern (80 marks, 3 hours).** This follows the ER-2020 board theory paper scheme. Confirm the pattern with your college, because the board may change the number and type of questions.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective (multiple-choice) questions — answer all 20 | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Short answers — answer any 10 of 11 | 10 × 3 = 30 |
| C | Long answers — answer any 6 of 7 | 6 × 5 = 30 |

In this guide, long questions carry 5 marks, short questions 3 marks, and a few 2-mark very short questions are kept for quick revision. A 3-mark answer needs about half a page: definition, source and three or four key points. A 5-mark answer needs about a page with headings.

## Where the marks come from

Chapter 5 (crude drug monographs) carries 30 of the 75 teaching hours, so expect **at least one long question and several short notes from it**. Chapters 3 (quality control), 4 (phytoconstituents) and 7 (traditional systems and Ayurvedic dosage forms) are the next most important. Chapters 1, 8 and 12 are short and usually appear as short answers or objective questions.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — appears in most years in some form; prepare the full answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for very short answers and as a backup choice.

The ratings are estimates from the syllabus weight and the kind of questions commonly set in D.Pharm Pharmacognosy papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

## Scoring tips for Pharmacognosy

1. **Use the monograph headings** for every drug: synonyms, biological source, family, geographical source, chemical constituents, uses, adulterants, test. Each heading earns marks even if one detail is wrong.
2. **Write the biological source completely**: part used + botanical name + author + family. "Dried leaflets of *Cassia angustifolia* Vahl, family Leguminosae" scores; "senna plant" does not.
3. **Underline botanical names** in the answer sheet (you cannot italicise by hand). Write the genus with a capital letter and the species in small letters.
4. **Name the active principle** in bold or underline: sennosides, digitoxin, quinine, reserpine, piperine, eugenol.
5. **Give one chemical test** wherever you know it (Borntrager's, Keller–Killiani, Vitali–Morin, murexide, thalleioquin). Examiners value it.
6. **Draw simple diagrams** for TS questions and for flow charts (alkaloid isolation, phytochemical investigation, evaluation of crude drugs).
7. For "classification" questions, give the **basis, examples, merits and demerits** of each system.
8. For Ayurvedic dosage forms, write **definition → method step by step → end point/tests → examples**.
9. In very short and objective questions, one exact fact is enough — botanical name, family or chief constituent.
10. Revise the **"Remember"** list at the end of each chapter and the last-night revision sheet before the exam.

## Suggested study plan (6 weeks)

| Week | Chapters |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 1, 2, 3 |
| 2 | 4, and 5 (laxatives, cardiotonics, carminatives) |
| 3 | 5 (astringents, nervous system, antihypertensive, antitussives, antirheumatic, antitumour) |
| 4 | 5 (antidiabetics to pharmaceutical aids, miscellaneous) |
| 5 | 6, 7, 8 |
| 6 | 9, 10, 11, 12, then mock paper and revision sheet |

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, revise these five areas with full answers: **evaluation of crude drugs and adulteration**, **classification of drugs**, **monographs of senna, digitalis, cinchona, rauwolfia, opium and clove**, **tests for alkaloids and glycosides**, and **Ayurvedic dosage forms (asava–arishta, bhasma, taila)**.

## Chapter 1–3 in ten lines

- Pharmacognosy = *pharmakon* (drug) + *gnosis* (knowledge); Schmidt 1811, Seydler 1815.
- Organised drugs have cells (leaf, bark, root); unorganised drugs do not (gum, resin, latex, oil).
- Six classifications: alphabetical (pharmacopoeias), taxonomical, morphological, pharmacological, chemical, chemo-taxonomical.
- Evaluation: morphological, microscopical, physical, chemical, biological.
- Stomatal index = S ÷ (S + E) × 100. Lycopodium spores ≈ 94,000 per mg.
- Acid-insoluble ash = sand and earth; water-soluble ash helps detect exhausted drugs.
- Bioassay: digitalis (pigeon/frog heart), ergot.

## Classic adulterants

## Chapter 6–12 key points

- **Cotton**: seed hairs of *Gossypium*, cellulose, twisted ribbons. **Silk**: fibroin + sericin, no sulphur. **Wool**: keratin with sulphur, scaly. **Viscose**: regenerated cellulose.
- **Catgut**: collagen from sheep intestine submucosa; absorbable; chromic = slower.
- **Ayurveda**: tridosha (vata, pitta, kapha), panchamahabhuta. **Unani**: four humours (dam, balgham, safra, sauda). **Siddha**: 96 thathuvas, Agastya. **Homoeopathy**: Hahnemann 1796, similia similibus curentur.
- **Asava** = juice, no boiling, fermented; **Arishta** = decoction, fermented; fermenting agent Dhataki flowers. **Bhasma** = shodhana + marana; tests rekhapurnatva, varitara. **Taila** kalka : oil : drava = 1 : 4 : 16.
- **Exports**: isabgol, senna, guar gum, mint oil, spices; NMPB (2000).
- **Nutraceutical** coined by DeFelice (1989). Probiotics = live microbes; prebiotics = inulin, FOS. Omega-3: ALA, EPA, DHA. Spirulina protein-rich. Garlic: alliin → allicin.
- **Herbal formulations**: traditional, modern, novel (phytosomes); Schedule T = GMP for ASU drugs.
- **Herbal cosmetics**: aloe gel (acemannan), almond oil (oleic), lavender (linalyl acetate), olive (oleic, squalene), rosemary (cineole, camphor), sandalwood (santalols).
- **Phytochemical investigation**: authenticate → extract (increasing polarity) → screen → chromatograph → purify → UV, IR, NMR, MS. Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent front distance.

## Common MCQ traps

- Clove is a **flower bud**, not a fruit; mother clove is the fruit.
- Black catechu = **heartwood** extract (Leguminosae); pale catechu = **leaf** extract (Rubiaceae).
- Ergot is a **fungal sclerotium** on rye.
- Ephedrine has **nitrogen outside the ring** (protoalkaloid).
- Colchicine is almost **neutral**, not strongly basic.
- Aloin is a **C-glycoside**, so ordinary Borntrager's test needs prior ferric chloride hydrolysis.
- Lanolin is a **wax**, not a glyceride.
- Silk has **no sulphur**; wool does.
- Asava is **not boiled**; arishta uses a **decoction**.

# Morphology of seeds and fruits: Ispaghula, Coriander, Fennel, Cardamom, Nutmeg, Black Pepper, Gokhru

**Aim:** To identify the given crude drugs (seeds and fruits) by their morphological (organoleptic) characters.

> Use the specimens from the college museum and compare with authentic samples. Follow your lab manual where it differs.

## Principle

Each crude drug has fixed external characters — shape, size, colour, surface, odour and taste — that do not change much from sample to sample. Studying them with the naked eye and a hand lens identifies the drug and shows gross adulteration. This is the first step of evaluation (organoleptic evaluation).

## Requirements

Specimens of the seven drugs, hand lens (magnifying glass), forceps, scale (ruler), white tile or paper, beaker of water (for ispaghula swelling and floating tests), blade.

## Procedure

1. Place each drug on white paper and note its general shape and colour.
2. Measure the length and breadth of five to ten pieces with the scale and record the range.
3. Examine the surface with a hand lens for ridges, wrinkles, furrows, spines and scars.
4. Break or cut one piece and observe the inside.
5. Crush a little between the fingers and smell it.
6. Taste a very small piece (only drugs known to be safe; never taste unknown drugs) and spit it out.
7. For ispaghula, put a few seeds in water and observe after 15–30 minutes.
8. Record observations in the table and draw a labelled sketch of each.

## Observations

| Feature | Ispaghula | Coriander | Fennel | Cardamom (seed) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Part | Seed | Fruit (cremocarp) | Fruit (cremocarp, often split) | Seeds within capsule |
| Shape | Boat-shaped (ovate-oblong), concave on one side | Nearly globular | Elongated, slightly curved | Capsule ovoid, three-sided; seeds angular |
| Size | About 2–3 mm long | About 2–4 mm diameter | About 5–10 mm long | Capsule 1–2 cm; seed about 3–4 mm |
| Colour | Pinkish-grey to brown | Brownish-yellow | Greenish-yellow to greenish-brown | Capsule pale green/buff; seeds reddish-brown |
| Surface | Smooth; convex side with a brown streak; whitish membrane on concave side | 10 wavy primary and 8 straight secondary ridges; calyx teeth and stylopod at top | Each mericarp with 5 prominent straight ridges | Capsule finely striated; seeds wrinkled, with membranous aril |
| Odour | None | Aromatic | Aromatic, anise-like | Strongly aromatic |
| Taste | Bland, mucilaginous | Spicy, aromatic | Sweet, aromatic | Aromatic, slightly pungent |
| Special | Swells in water forming mucilage | Mericarps do not separate easily | Mericarps often separate | — |

| Feature | Nutmeg | Black pepper | Gokhru |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Part | Seed kernel | Unripe fruit (drupe) | Fruit (schizocarp) |
| Shape | Ovoid to ellipsoid | Globular | Five-angled, made of 5 wedge-shaped cocci |
| Size | About 2–3 cm long | About 3.5–6 mm diameter | About 1 cm across |
| Colour | Greyish-brown (may be lime-coated white) | Dark brown to black | Greenish-yellow to greyish |
| Surface | Network of shallow furrows (reticulately furrowed) | Coarsely wrinkled network; scar of stalk | Each coccus with 2 pairs of hard spines (one longer pair) |
| Inside | Marbled cut surface — dark perisperm folds in pale endosperm (ruminate endosperm) | Hard, whitish centre | Seeds within hard cocci |
| Odour | Strongly aromatic | Aromatic | None |
| Taste | Warm, aromatic, slightly bitter | Very pungent | Slightly astringent |

```text
   Ispaghula seed        Coriander fruit       Fennel mericarp       Gokhru fruit
     ______               ___________               /\                  \ /
    /      \             /  ~~~~~~~  \             /  \               -- * --
   (  ____  )           |  ~~~~~~~~~  |           | || |              / \ / \
    \______/   ← boat    \___________/            | || |  ← 5 ridges     spines
   concave side            wavy ridges            \____/
```

## Result

The given drugs were identified as: ispaghula, coriander, fennel, cardamom, nutmeg, black pepper and gokhru, from their morphological characters recorded above.

## Precautions

1. Use a clean, well-lit surface and a good hand lens.
2. Measure several pieces and give a range, not a single value.
3. Taste only safe, edible drugs and only a tiny amount; spit out and rinse the mouth.
4. Do not mix specimens; return each to its labelled jar.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a cremocarp?** A dry fruit of the Umbelliferae that splits into two one-seeded halves called mericarps (coriander, fennel).
2. **Which part of ispaghula forms mucilage?** The outer epidermis of the seed coat (the husk).
3. **What is mace?** The dried arillus that surrounds the nutmeg seed.
4. **Name the adulterant of black pepper.** Dried papaya seeds; they are lighter, less wrinkled and not pungent.
5. **How do you tell coriander from fennel?** Coriander is globular with wavy and straight ridges and mericarps that stay joined; fennel is elongated with five straight ridges per mericarp.
6. **Why is nutmeg sometimes coated with lime?** To protect it from insects during storage.
7. **What is "large gokhru"?** Fruits of *Pedalium murex*, used as a substitute for *Tribulus terrestris*.
8. **Name the chief constituent of fennel oil.** Anethole (with fenchone).
practicals.title: Morphology of seeds and fruits: Ispaghula, Coriander, Fennel, Cardamom, Nutmeg, Black Pepper, Gokhru

practicals.markdown:
# Morphology of leaves, flower buds and herbs: Senna, Clove, Ephedra, Punarnava

**Aim:** To identify senna, clove, ephedra and punarnava by their morphological characters.

> Use museum specimens and compare with authentic samples. Follow your lab manual where it differs.

## Principle

Leaves, flower buds, stems and whole herbs have characteristic shape, size, apex, base, margin, venation, surface, colour, odour and taste. Recording these identifies the drug and helps detect substitutes (for example *Cassia auriculata* in senna, or stalks and mother cloves in clove).

## Requirements

Specimens of senna leaflets, clove, ephedra stems and punarnava (whole plant), hand lens, scale, forceps, white paper, beaker of water, blade.

## Procedure

1. Spread each specimen on white paper and note the general form and colour.
2. For senna, examine the shape, apex, base, margin and venation of five leaflets and measure them.
3. For clove, measure the length, identify the hypanthium, sepals and the head of petals; press the hypanthium with a fingernail to see oil come out; drop a few cloves into water.
4. For ephedra, observe stem thickness, ridges, nodes and scale leaves.
5. For punarnava, observe root, stem, nodes, leaves and any flowers or fruits.
6. Note odour and taste (tiny amount; spit out).
7. Record observations and draw labelled sketches.

## Observations

| Feature | Senna (leaflet) | Clove (flower bud) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | Lanceolate | Nail-shaped: cylindrical hypanthium with a rounded head |
| Size | About 2.5–5 cm long, 0.7–1.5 cm wide (Indian senna) | About 10–17.5 mm long |
| Colour | Pale yellowish-green | Dark brown to crimson-brown |
| Apex / head | Acute, with a small sharp point (mucronate) | Four thick sepals around a dome of four unopened petals |
| Base | **Asymmetric** (unequal) | Hypanthium tapering below |
| Margin / surface | Entire margin; pinnate venation; fine hairs | Hypanthium wrinkled; oil exudes when pressed with a nail |
| Odour | Faint, characteristic | Strongly aromatic |
| Taste | Mucilaginous, then slightly bitter | Pungent, aromatic, numbing |
| Special | — | Good cloves sink or float upright in water; exhausted cloves float flat |

| Feature | Ephedra (stem) | Punarnava (whole plant) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Form | Slender, cylindrical, jointed green stems | Diffuse, spreading herb with a thick root |
| Size | About 1–2 mm thick; internodes a few centimetres long | Root several cm long, up to about 1–2 cm thick |
| Colour | Green to yellowish-green | Root yellowish-brown; stem often purplish |
| Surface | Fine longitudinal ridges and furrows | Stem with swollen nodes; leaves opposite, unequal, ovate, green above and whitish below |
| Nodes | Two small scale leaves at each node, joined at the base into a sheath | Small pink flowers in clusters; small ribbed sticky fruits |
| Odour | Slight | Not distinct |
| Taste | Astringent, slightly bitter | Slightly bitter |

```text
  Senna leaflet               Clove                     Ephedra stem
      /\  ← acute,             ___
     /  \   mucronate         (   )  ← head of petals     |
    | /\ |                    /| |\  ← 4 sepals           =|=  ← node with
    |/  \|  pinnate veins       | |                        |     scale leaves
     \  /                       | |  ← hypanthium          |
  ___/  \  ← unequal base       |_|                        |
```

## Result

The given drugs were identified as senna, clove, ephedra and punarnava from their morphological characters.

## Precautions

1. Handle dry leaflets gently; they break easily.
2. Examine several specimens and record ranges.
3. Taste only a tiny amount of safe drugs and spit out; do not taste ephedra in quantity.
4. Return specimens to their labelled containers.

## Viva questions

1. **Give the biological source of senna.** Dried leaflets of *Cassia angustifolia* (Indian) and *Cassia acutifolia* (Alexandrian); Leguminosae.
2. **Which feature of senna leaflet is most diagnostic?** The asymmetric base.
3. **Name an adulterant of senna and a test for it.** *Cassia auriculata* (Palthe senna); it gives a red colour with 80% sulphuric acid.
4. **What part of clove is used?** The dried flower bud.
5. **What are mother cloves?** The ripe fruits of the clove plant, used as an adulterant.
6. **Why do exhausted cloves float flat in water?** Their oil has been removed, so they are lighter.
7. **Name the chief alkaloid of ephedra and its use.** Ephedrine; bronchodilator in asthma and nasal decongestant.
8. **Give the botanical name and family of punarnava.** *Boerhaavia diffusa*, Nyctaginaceae; used as a diuretic.
practicals.title: Morphology of leaves, flower buds and herbs: Senna, Clove, Ephedra, Punarnava

# Morphology of barks, underground parts and agar: Cinnamon, Cinchona, Ginger, Rauwolfia, Agar

**Aim:** To identify cinnamon, cinchona, ginger, rauwolfia and agar by their morphological characters.

> Use museum specimens and compare with authentic samples. Follow your lab manual where it differs.

## Principle

Barks are described by shape (flat, curved, quill, double quill, compound quill), thickness, outer and inner surface, fracture, odour and taste. Roots and rhizomes are described by shape, branching, surface marks, fracture and the appearance of the cut surface. Agar, an unorganised drug, is described by form, colour, texture and behaviour in water.

```text
Shapes of bark pieces

 Flat      Curved     Channelled    Quill      Double quill   Compound quill
 ____       ___         _____        ( )          ( )( )         ((( )))
              \__        \___/                                 quills inside quills
                                                               (cinnamon)
```

## Requirements

Specimens of cinnamon, cinchona, ginger, rauwolfia and agar; hand lens; scale; blade; white paper; beaker; hot water bath; test tube.

## Procedure

1. Note the shape and size of each drug; measure the bark thickness.
2. Examine the outer and inner surfaces of the barks with a hand lens.
3. Break a piece and note the fracture (short, fibrous, splintery, granular).
4. Cut ginger and rauwolfia transversely and look at the cut surface.
5. Smell and taste (tiny amount; spit out).
6. For agar, note the form; soak a piece in cold water; boil 1 g in 100 ml water, then cool and observe.
7. Record and sketch.

## Observations

| Feature | Cinnamon | Cinchona |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | **Compound quills** (several thin quills packed one inside another) | Quills, curved or channelled pieces |
| Thickness | Thin, about 0.5 mm | Thicker, about 2–6 mm |
| Outer surface | Light yellowish-brown with fine wavy lines and small scars | Greyish-brown (reddish-brown in red bark), often with lichens; longitudinal and transverse cracks |
| Inner surface | Darker brown, finely striated | Reddish-brown, finely striated |
| Fracture | Splintery | Short in outer part, fibrous in inner part |
| Odour | Fragrant, sweet | Slight |
| Taste | Warm, sweet and aromatic | Intensely **bitter** and astringent |

| Feature | Ginger | Rauwolfia |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Part | Rhizome | Root |
| Shape | Branched in one plane like fingers of a hand ("hands" or "races"), laterally flattened | Cylindrical, slightly tortuous pieces, few rootlets |
| Size | About 5–15 cm long | About 5–15 cm long, up to about 2 cm thick |
| Surface | Buff; scraped ginger smooth with longitudinal lines; unscraped shows cork and leaf scars | Greyish-yellow to light brown; longitudinally wrinkled; bark peels easily |
| Fracture | Short and fibrous; cut surface shows a ring (endodermis) and yellowish dots of oil cells | Short; thin bark and dense pale-yellow wood |
| Odour | Aromatic | Indistinct |
| Taste | Pungent, warm | Bitter |

| Feature | Agar |
| --- | --- |
| Form | Thin translucent strips, flakes, sheets or powder |
| Colour | Yellowish-white to pale yellow |
| Texture | Tough when damp, brittle when dry; surface wrinkled |
| Odour / taste | Odourless; mucilaginous taste |
| Behaviour in water | Insoluble in cold water but swells; dissolves in boiling water; a 1% solution sets into a firm gel on cooling |

## Result

The drugs were identified as cinnamon (compound quills), cinchona (bitter bark), ginger (rhizome), rauwolfia (root) and agar (algal product).

## Precautions

1. Measure bark thickness at several places.
2. Do not confuse cinnamon with cassia bark, which is thicker, coarser and in single quills.
3. Taste only a tiny amount; rauwolfia is bitter and pharmacologically active — spit out and rinse.
4. Use clean glassware for the agar gel test.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a compound quill?** A bark rolled into a quill with several smaller quills packed inside it, as in cinnamon.
2. **What is the main adulterant of cinnamon?** Cassia bark (*Cinnamomum cassia*).
3. **Name the alkaloids of cinchona.** Quinine, quinidine, cinchonine and cinchonidine.
4. **What is Grahe's test?** Cinchona bark heated in a dry test tube gives red tarry vapours.
5. **Why are ginger pieces called hands?** The rhizome branches in one plane like the fingers of a hand.
6. **Give the source of agar.** Red algae such as *Gelidium amansii* and *Gracilaria* species.
7. **Give one use of agar in a laboratory.** Solid culture medium for bacteria.
8. **Name the antihypertensive alkaloid of rauwolfia.** Reserpine.
practicals.title: Morphology of barks, underground parts and agar: Cinnamon, Cinchona, Ginger, Rauwolfia, Agar

# Transverse section of leaves: Datura and Vasaka

**Aim:** To prepare, stain and study the transverse section (TS) of the leaves of datura and vasaka, and to identify their diagnostic characters.

> Follow your lab manual for the staining schedule. Handle razor blades with care.

## Principle

The internal structure (anatomy) of a leaf is constant for a species. A thin transverse section through the midrib, cleared and stained, shows the epidermis, trichomes, stomata, mesophyll, vascular bundle and cell inclusions. **Phloroglucinol with conc. HCl** stains lignified walls (xylem) pink-red; **chloral hydrate** clears the tissue by dissolving starch and chlorophyll.

## Requirements

Fresh or soaked leaves (or leaf pieces fixed in a potato or carrot block), sharp razor blade, watch glasses, brush, glass slides and cover slips, chloral hydrate solution, phloroglucinol solution (1% in alcohol), conc. HCl, dilute glycerine, compound microscope, spirit lamp.

## Procedure

1. Soak a dry leaf in water (or boil briefly) to soften it.
2. Hold a piece of the leaf with the midrib between two pieces of potato or pith.
3. Cut many very thin sections at right angles to the midrib with a wet razor, using one smooth stroke.
4. Transfer sections to a watch glass of water with a brush; select the thinnest complete ones.
5. Clear: warm the section in chloral hydrate on a slide for a few minutes.
6. Stain: add a drop of phloroglucinol, wait a minute, add a drop of conc. HCl.
7. Mount in dilute glycerine, place a cover slip without air bubbles.
8. Observe under low power, then high power. Draw a labelled diagram (outline of the whole TS plus a detailed sector).

## Observations

| Tissue | Datura leaf | Vasaka leaf |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type of leaf | Dorsiventral | Dorsiventral |
| Epidermis | Single layer with cuticle on both surfaces | Single layer with cuticle; some cells contain **cystoliths** (calcium carbonate bodies) |
| Trichomes | **Covering**: uniseriate, multicellular, warty (2–5 cells). **Glandular**: short stalk with multicellular head | Covering: uniseriate, few-celled; glandular trichomes present |
| Stomata | **Anisocytic** (cruciferous), on both surfaces | **Diacytic** (caryophyllaceous), mainly on lower surface |
| Palisade | Single layer under the upper epidermis, not continuous over the midrib | One or two layers, not continuous over the midrib |
| Spongy mesophyll | Loosely arranged; many cells with **cluster crystals** of calcium oxalate; some microcrystals | Loose spongy cells |
| Midrib | Collenchyma under both epidermises; **bicollateral** vascular bundle (phloem above and below the xylem arc) | Collenchyma under both epidermises; crescent-shaped collateral vascular bundle |
| Other | — | **Acicular (needle-like) crystals** of calcium oxalate in parenchyma |

```text
TS of Datura leaf through midrib (outline)

  cuticle  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
  upper epidermis  ▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯ (warty hair)  ▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯
  palisade         ||||||||||                ||||||||
  spongy (o = cluster crystal) o    o   (   )   o
  lower epidermis  ▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯ stoma ▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯▯
                              _____
                   collenchyma(phloem)
                             ( xylem )   ← bicollateral bundle
                             (phloem )
                              ‾‾‾‾‾
```

## Result

The section showing anisocytic stomata, warty covering trichomes, glandular trichomes, cluster crystals and a bicollateral bundle was identified as **datura leaf**. The section showing diacytic stomata, cystoliths and acicular crystals was identified as **vasaka leaf**.

## Precautions

1. Sections must be thin, complete and cut at right angles to the midrib.
2. Do not let sections dry; keep them in water.
3. Do not overheat chloral hydrate (bubbles spoil the mount).
4. Add HCl after phloroglucinol, not before; wipe off excess acid to protect the microscope.
5. Remove air bubbles before observing.

## Viva questions

1. **Why is chloral hydrate used?** It clears the section by dissolving starch, chlorophyll and proteins, so cell walls and crystals are seen clearly.
2. **What does phloroglucinol + HCl stain?** Lignified walls (xylem, fibres, stone cells) pink-red.
3. **What is a bicollateral vascular bundle?** A bundle with phloem on both the outer and inner side of the xylem, as in Solanaceae.
4. **What type of stomata does datura have?** Anisocytic — three subsidiary cells, one smaller than the other two.
5. **What are cystoliths?** Deposits of calcium carbonate on a stalk inside enlarged epidermal cells, typical of Acanthaceae (vasaka).
6. **Name the alkaloid of vasaka.** Vasicine.
7. **Name the family of datura and its alkaloids.** Solanaceae; hyoscyamine and hyoscine.
8. **What are diacytic stomata?** Stomata with two subsidiary cells at right angles to the guard cells.
practicals.title: Transverse section of leaves: Datura and Vasaka

practicals.markdown:
# Transverse section of fruits and seeds: Ajwain, Coriander and Nux-vomica

**Aim:** To prepare and study the transverse sections of ajwain fruit, coriander fruit and nux-vomica seed, and to note their diagnostic characters.

> Follow your lab manual for the staining schedule. Nux-vomica is very poisonous (strychnine): never taste it, and wash hands after handling.

## Principle

Fruits of the Umbelliferae (ajwain, coriander) are cremocarps; a TS of one mericarp shows the pericarp with **vittae** (oil canals), vascular bundles at the ridges, the seed coat and a large oily endosperm. The number and position of vittae and the presence of sclerenchyma help to tell them apart. Nux-vomica seed has a testa of characteristic **lignified hairs** and a hard horny endosperm.

## Requirements

Ajwain and coriander fruits (soaked overnight), nux-vomica seeds (soaked or boiled until soft — they are very hard), razor blade, potato or pith block, chloral hydrate, phloroglucinol (1% alcoholic), conc. HCl, iodine solution, dilute glycerine, slides, cover slips, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Soften the fruits and seeds (soaking; nux-vomica needs long soaking or boiling).
2. Fix a single mericarp (or seed) in a potato block and cut thin transverse sections through the middle.
3. Clear in warm chloral hydrate.
4. Stain with phloroglucinol + conc. HCl; for nux-vomica also test a section with iodine (protein and aleurone stain yellow-brown).
5. Mount in dilute glycerine and observe under low and high power.
6. Draw labelled diagrams.

## Observations

| Tissue | Ajwain (*Trachyspermum ammi*) fruit | Coriander (*Coriandrum sativum*) fruit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outline of mericarp | Pentagonal; surface with many small **papillae** (warty outgrowths) | Curved arc (half of a globular fruit); wavy outline from ridges |
| Epicarp | Single layer of cells, papillose | Single layer with cuticle; small crystals of calcium oxalate |
| Mesocarp | Parenchyma with **vittae**: usually 4 on the dorsal side and 2 on the commissural side | Thick band of **lignified sclerenchyma** (fibres) — characteristic; dorsal vittae absent or reduced; **2 vittae on the commissural side** |
| Vascular bundles | Small bundles under each primary ridge | Small bundles at the primary ridges |
| Endocarp | Thin-walled cells | Thin, elongated cells |
| Seed coat | Brown layer of thin cells | Brown thin layer |
| Endosperm | Large, polygonal cells with fixed oil and aleurone grains | Curved (concave towards the commissure), cells with fixed oil, aleurone grains and small **rosette crystals** of calcium oxalate |
| Embryo | Small, at the top of the endosperm | Small |

| Tissue | Nux-vomica (*Strychnos nux-vomica*) seed |
| --- | --- |
| Testa (epidermis) | Each epidermal cell grows into a long, thick-walled, **lignified covering hair**, bent at the base and lying flat, with longitudinal thickening bars; stains pink with phloroglucinol |
| Below epidermis | Collapsed, brown layer of cells |
| Endosperm | Large, thick-walled cells with walls of hemicellulose, showing fine **plasmodesmata**; contains oil globules and aleurone grains; no starch |
| Embryo | Small, in a cavity in the endosperm |

```text
TS of coriander mericarp (outline)

        ~~~~~~~ wavy epicarp ~~~~~~~
      ////// sclerenchyma band //////     ← stains pink
     (   endosperm, curved, oily    )
      \_____     ( O )  ( O )  ____/      ← 2 commissural vittae
             commissural surface
```

## Result

The sections were identified as ajwain fruit (papillose epicarp, six vittae), coriander fruit (thick sclerenchyma band, two commissural vittae, curved endosperm) and nux-vomica seed (lignified bent hairs, thick-walled endosperm with plasmodesmata).

## Precautions

1. Cut sections through the middle of the fruit or seed so that all tissues appear.
2. Do not taste nux-vomica; it contains strychnine and brucine.
3. Clear well before staining; wipe off excess acid.
4. Use a fresh, sharp blade for the hard nux-vomica seed.

## Viva questions

1. **What are vittae?** Schizogenous oil canals in the pericarp of Umbelliferous fruits.
2. **How many vittae are seen in a coriander mericarp?** Two, on the commissural side; dorsal vittae are absent or rudimentary.
3. **Which tissue of coriander stains pink with phloroglucinol?** The sclerenchyma band in the mesocarp.
4. **What is the volatile oil constituent of ajwain?** Thymol.
5. **Give the alkaloids of nux-vomica.** Strychnine and brucine.
6. **What are plasmodesmata?** Fine strands of cytoplasm passing through pores in cell walls, seen in the endosperm of nux-vomica.
7. **What is the nature of the hairs on nux-vomica seed?** Lignified, thick-walled covering trichomes bent at the base.
8. **What is the commissural surface?** The flat inner surface where the two mericarps of a cremocarp are joined.
practicals.title: Transverse section of fruits and seeds: Ajwain, Coriander and Nux-vomica

practicals.markdown:
# Transverse section of clove (flower bud)

**Aim:** To prepare and study the transverse section of the hypanthium of clove and identify its diagnostic characters.

> Follow your lab manual for the staining schedule. Handle razor blades with care.

## Principle

Clove is the dried flower bud of *Syzygium aromaticum* (Myrtaceae). Its stalk-like lower part, the **hypanthium**, contains many large **schizolysigenous oil glands** near the surface, a spongy aerenchyma in the middle and a central columella with vascular bundles. These features, with the strong aromatic oil, identify clove and its powder.

## Requirements

Cloves soaked in water for a few hours, potato block, razor blade, watch glass, brush, chloral hydrate, phloroglucinol (1% alcoholic), conc. HCl, Sudan red III (optional, for oil), dilute glycerine, slides, cover slips, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Soak cloves in water so the hypanthium becomes soft.
2. Fix the hypanthium in a potato block and cut thin transverse sections through its middle.
3. Clear in warm chloral hydrate (oil glands may look empty after clearing; for oil, stain an uncleared section with Sudan red III).
4. Stain with phloroglucinol and conc. HCl.
5. Mount in dilute glycerine; observe under low and high power.
6. Draw an outline diagram and a detailed sector.

## Observations

| Zone (outside → inside) | Character |
| --- | --- |
| Epidermis | Single layer of small cells with a very thick cuticle; a few stomata |
| Outer cortex (oil gland zone) | Parenchyma with **2–3 rows of large oval schizolysigenous oil glands** arranged in a ring just below the epidermis |
| Middle cortex | Parenchyma with a ring of small **bicollateral vascular bundles**, each with a few pericyclic fibres; cluster crystals of calcium oxalate |
| Aerenchyma | Loose tissue with large air spaces (spongy zone) |
| Central columella | Dense parenchyma with a ring of small vascular bundles and many **cluster crystals** |
| Stains | Lignified fibres and xylem pink-red; oil glands red with Sudan red III |

```text
TS of clove hypanthium (outline)

            thick cuticle + epidermis
        ( O  O  O  O  O  O  O  O  O )   ← oil glands, 2–3 rows
        (  · · · · · · · · · · · ·   )   ← ring of vascular bundles
        (   ° ° ° aerenchyma ° ° °    )   ← air spaces
        (      [ columella with   ]   )
        (      [ bundles + crystals]  )
```

**Quantitative note (optional):** count the oil glands visible in one quadrant of the section and multiply by four to estimate the number per section; compare with a known good sample.

## Result

The section showing a thick cuticle, rows of large oil glands below the epidermis, a ring of bicollateral bundles, aerenchyma and a central columella with cluster crystals was identified as **clove (hypanthium)**.

## Precautions

1. Cut through the hypanthium, not through the head.
2. Sections must be thin and complete.
3. Do not overheat during clearing; oil may be lost.
4. Remove air bubbles before observation.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the hypanthium?** The cup-like, stalk-shaped part of the flower below the sepals, formed by the fused base of floral parts.
2. **What type of oil glands occur in clove?** Schizolysigenous oil glands.
3. **Name the chief constituent of clove oil.** Eugenol.
4. **What is aerenchyma?** Spongy parenchyma with large air spaces.
5. **What are the adulterants of clove?** Clove stalks, mother cloves (fruits), blown cloves and exhausted cloves.
6. **How do clove stalks differ under the microscope?** They have stone cells (sclereids), which are absent in good clove buds.
7. **What crystals are seen in clove?** Cluster crystals (rosettes) of calcium oxalate.
8. **Why is clove oil used in dentistry?** Eugenol is antiseptic and has a local anaesthetic (numbing) effect.
practicals.title: Transverse section of clove (flower bud)

practicals.markdown:
# Transverse section of barks: Cinnamon and Cinchona

**Aim:** To prepare and study the transverse sections of cinnamon bark and cinchona bark and to compare their diagnostic characters.

> Follow your lab manual for the staining schedule. Handle razor blades with care.

## Principle

Barks consist of tissues outside the cambium: cork, cortex, pericycle and secondary phloem with medullary rays. The type and arrangement of **stone cells, fibres, crystals, oil cells and starch** differ between barks. Phloroglucinol + HCl stains lignified stone cells and fibres pink-red; iodine stains starch blue.

## Requirements

Pieces of cinnamon and cinchona bark soaked in water (or boiled briefly), potato block, razor blade, chloral hydrate, phloroglucinol (1% alcoholic), conc. HCl, iodine solution, dilute glycerine, slides, cover slips, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Soften the bark pieces by soaking or boiling.
2. Cut thin transverse sections across the bark (at right angles to its length).
3. Mount one section in iodine to see starch.
4. Clear another section in chloral hydrate, stain with phloroglucinol + conc. HCl and mount in dilute glycerine.
5. Observe under low and high power; draw labelled diagrams.

## Observations

| Tissue (outside → inside) | Cinnamon bark | Cinchona bark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cork | Absent (outer bark is scraped off in preparation) | Present: several layers of thin-walled, reddish-brown cork cells |
| Cortex | Mostly removed | Parenchyma with starch, **idioblasts filled with microcrystals (sandy crystals)** of calcium oxalate; some secretion cells |
| Pericycle | A nearly **continuous ring of stone cells (sclereids)** with groups of **pericyclic fibres** — very characteristic | No continuous ring of stone cells |
| Secondary phloem | Sieve tissue, phloem parenchyma, **isolated lignified phloem fibres**, many **oil cells** and **mucilage cells**, starch grains | Many **large, isolated, spindle-shaped phloem fibres** with very thick, striated, lignified walls and funnel-shaped pits; phloem parenchyma with starch and microcrystals |
| Medullary rays | 1–2 cells wide, cells contain small **acicular crystals** of calcium oxalate | 1–3 cells wide, widening outwards |
| Stone cells | Present (pericycle ring) | Absent or very few |
| With phloroglucinol + HCl | Stone-cell ring and fibres pink | Phloem fibres pink |

```text
TS of cinnamon bark (sector)               TS of cinchona bark (sector)

 ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓  ← stone-cell ring          ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒  ← cork
  ◆   ◆      ◆      pericyclic fibres          ·  ✷   ·   ← cortex, idioblast
  o   |  ◇   |  o   ← oil cell (o),            ●  |  ●   |   ← big isolated
  ◇   |  o   |  ◇     mucilage cell (◇)        ·  |   ●  |      phloem fibres
      |      |      ← medullary rays              |      |   ← rays
```

## Result

The section with a continuous pericyclic ring of stone cells, oil and mucilage cells and acicular crystals in narrow rays is **cinnamon bark**. The section with cork, idioblasts of microcrystals, large isolated thick-walled phloem fibres and no stone cells is **cinchona bark**.

## Precautions

1. Cut sections exactly across the bark.
2. Sections should be thin; thick ones hide the stone cells.
3. Use iodine on a separate, uncleared section for starch.
4. Wipe off excess acid after staining.

## Viva questions

1. **What is the most diagnostic feature of cinnamon bark?** A continuous ring of stone cells in the pericycle.
2. **Why is cork absent in cinnamon of commerce?** The outer bark is scraped off before drying.
3. **What crystals are present in cinnamon bark?** Small acicular (needle) crystals of calcium oxalate in the medullary rays.
4. **Describe the phloem fibres of cinchona.** Large, spindle-shaped, isolated, very thick-walled and lignified, with striations and funnel-shaped pits.
5. **What are idioblasts?** Single cells different from their neighbours, here filled with microcrystals of calcium oxalate.
6. **How do you tell cassia bark from cinnamon?** Cassia is thicker, has cork, a broken (not continuous) stone-cell layer and more starch.
7. **Name the antimalarial alkaloid of cinchona.** Quinine.
8. **What is the use of phloroglucinol in this experiment?** It stains lignified stone cells and fibres pink-red.
practicals.title: Transverse section of barks: Cinnamon and Cinchona

practicals.markdown:
# Transverse section of roots, stolons and rhizomes: Ashwagandha, Liquorice and Curcuma

**Aim:** To prepare and study the transverse sections of ashwagandha root, liquorice (root/stolon) and curcuma (turmeric) rhizome, and to note their diagnostic characters.

> Follow your lab manual for the staining schedule. Handle razor blades with care.

## Principle

Dicot roots and stolons with secondary growth (ashwagandha, liquorice) show cork, cortex or phelloderm, secondary phloem, cambium, secondary xylem and medullary rays. A monocot rhizome (curcuma) shows no cambium; its vascular bundles are scattered in a cortex and in a stele separated by an endodermis. Inclusions such as starch, crystal sheaths, oil cells and colouring matter help identify each drug.

## Requirements

Soaked pieces of ashwagandha root, liquorice and turmeric rhizome, potato block, razor blade, chloral hydrate, phloroglucinol (1% alcoholic), conc. HCl, iodine solution, dilute glycerine, slides, cover slips, microscope.

## Procedure

1. Soften the drugs by soaking (or brief boiling).
2. Cut thin transverse sections; keep them in water.
3. Mount one section of each in iodine to observe starch.
4. Clear another in chloral hydrate, stain with phloroglucinol + conc. HCl, mount in dilute glycerine.
5. Observe and draw labelled diagrams.

## Observations

| Tissue | Ashwagandha root (*Withania somnifera*) | Liquorice (*Glycyrrhiza glabra*) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cork | Thin layer of brownish cork cells | Several layers of **reddish-brown** cork (absent in peeled liquorice) |
| Cortex / phelloderm | Parenchyma **packed with starch grains**; some cells with microsphenoidal (sandy) crystals of calcium oxalate | Few layers of parenchyma with starch and some prismatic crystals |
| Secondary phloem | Narrow, with phloem parenchyma and starch | Wedge-shaped strands of phloem with **groups of lignified phloem fibres surrounded by a sheath of prismatic calcium oxalate crystals** (crystal sheath); wavy medullary rays |
| Cambium | Thin ring | Distinct ring |
| Secondary xylem | Vessels scattered in xylem parenchyma rich in starch; medullary rays | Large vessels, **xylem fibres with crystal sheath**, xylem parenchyma with starch; broad medullary rays |
| Pith | Absent (root) | Present in stolon; absent in root |

| Tissue | Curcuma (turmeric) rhizome (*Curcuma longa*) |
| --- | --- |
| Outer layer | Epidermis (often worn off) and a few layers of cork formed in the outer cortex |
| Cortex | Thin-walled parenchyma with **scattered closed collateral vascular bundles** and many **oil cells** with yellow oil |
| Endodermis | Distinct single layer separating cortex from stele |
| Stele | Parenchyma with numerous **scattered vascular bundles**, crowded just inside the endodermis |
| Cell contents | Parenchyma filled with **gelatinised starch** and yellow colouring matter (curcumin), so the section looks yellow |
| Cambium | Absent (monocot) |

```text
TS of curcuma rhizome (outline)

   cork ▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒
   cortex  · o ·  · o  ·    o  ·   ← scattered bundles (·), oil cells (o)
   ───────── endodermis ─────────
   stele  :::::::::::::::::::::     ← crowded bundles inside endodermis
          ·   ·    ·    ·    ·     ← scattered bundles, yellow parenchyma
```

## Result

The sections were identified as **ashwagandha root** (thin cork, starch-filled parenchyma, sandy crystals, no pith), **liquorice** (reddish-brown cork, phloem and xylem fibres with crystal sheaths, wavy rays) and **curcuma rhizome** (scattered closed bundles, endodermis, oil cells, yellow gelatinised starch).

## Precautions

1. Sections should be thin and include all tissues from outside to centre.
2. Turmeric stains fingers and slides yellow; wash promptly.
3. Do not over-clear sections meant for starch observation.
4. Wipe off excess acid after staining.

## Viva questions

1. **What is a crystal sheath?** A layer of cells, each with a prism of calcium oxalate, surrounding a group of fibres, as in liquorice.
2. **What is the sweet principle of liquorice?** Glycyrrhizin (a triterpenoid saponin glycoside).
3. **Why is the starch of turmeric gelatinised?** The rhizomes are boiled or steamed before drying.
4. **Is curcuma a monocot or dicot? How do you know?** Monocot; it has scattered closed vascular bundles and no cambium.
5. **Name the active constituents of ashwagandha.** Withanolides (such as withaferin A) and alkaloids.
6. **Name the yellow pigment of turmeric.** Curcumin.
7. **How is a stolon of liquorice told from a root?** The stolon has a pith; the root does not.
8. **Which reagent shows starch, and what colour?** Iodine solution; blue to blue-black.
practicals.title: Transverse section of roots, stolons and rhizomes: Ashwagandha, Liquorice and Curcuma

practicals.markdown:
# Physical and chemical tests: Acacia, Tragacanth, Agar, Guar gum and Gelatine

**Aim:** To identify acacia, tragacanth, agar, guar gum and gelatine by physical and chemical tests.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles and a lab coat.

## Principle

Acacia, tragacanth, agar and guar gum are **polysaccharides** (gums and mucilages); gelatine is a **protein**. They differ in how they behave in water (dissolve, swell or gel) and in their reactions:

- Carbohydrates give a violet ring with **Molisch's reagent**.
- Mucilages stain pink with **ruthenium red**.
- **Iodine** turns starch blue and gives a crimson colour with agar.
- Acacia contains **oxidase**, which turns guaiacum blue in the presence of hydrogen peroxide.
- Proteins (gelatine) are precipitated by **tannic acid** and **picric acid** and give a violet **biuret** reaction.

## Requirements

Powdered samples; test tubes, beakers, glass rods, water bath, spirit lamp; reagents — Molisch's reagent (α-naphthol in alcohol), conc. H2SO4, ruthenium red solution, N/50 iodine solution, lead subacetate solution, tincture of guaiacum, dilute hydrogen peroxide, 5% tannic acid, saturated picric acid, 10% NaOH, dilute copper sulphate, soda lime.

## Procedure and observations

**A. Physical behaviour**

| Test | Acacia | Tragacanth | Agar | Guar gum | Gelatine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appearance | White to yellowish tears or powder | White to pale yellow ribbons/flakes or powder | Yellowish-white strips or powder | Off-white powder | Colourless to pale yellow sheets or granules |
| 1 g + 10 ml cold water, shake | Dissolves slowly to a clear, sticky solution | Swells to a thick, gel-like mass | Swells, does not dissolve | Disperses to a very **viscous** solution | Swells, absorbs water |
| 1 g in 100 ml boiling water, then cool | — | — | Dissolves on boiling; **sets to a firm gel** on cooling | Viscous | Dissolves on warming; **sets to a gel** on cooling |

**B. Chemical tests**

| No. | Test | Acacia | Tragacanth | Agar | Guar gum | Gelatine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Molisch's test: solution + 2 drops Molisch's reagent, conc. H2SO4 poured down the side | Violet ring | Violet ring | Violet ring | Violet ring | No violet ring |
| 2 | Powder + ruthenium red on a slide | — | Pink (mucilage) | Pink | Pink | — |
| 3 | Powder or solution + N/50 iodine | No blue (no starch) | A few blue particles may appear (traces of starch) | **Crimson to brownish-purple** | No blue | — |
| 4 | Solution + lead subacetate | **White precipitate** | — | — | — | — |
| 5 | Solution + tincture of guaiacum + few drops H2O2 | **Blue colour** (oxidase) | No blue | No blue | No blue | — |
| 6 | Solution + 5% tannic acid | — | — | **No precipitate** | — | **Buff precipitate** |
| 7 | Solution + picric acid | — | — | — | — | **Yellow precipitate** |
| 8 | Biuret: solution + NaOH + dilute CuSO4 | — | — | — | — | **Violet colour** (protein) |
| 9 | Solid heated with soda lime | — | — | — | — | Smell of **ammonia** (nitrogen present) |

(— means the test is not used for identification of that sample.)

## Result

The samples were identified as:

- **Acacia** — dissolves in water; white precipitate with lead subacetate; blue with guaiacum + H2O2 (oxidase); no starch.
- **Tragacanth** — swells to a gel in cold water; pink with ruthenium red; traces of starch.
- **Agar** — gels on cooling after boiling; crimson with iodine; no precipitate with tannic acid.
- **Guar gum** — very viscous dispersion in cold water; Molisch-positive; pink with ruthenium red.
- **Gelatine** — gels on cooling; precipitates with tannic and picric acids; biuret-positive; ammonia with soda lime.

## Precautions

1. Add conc. H2SO4 slowly along the side of the tube; do not shake.
2. Use freshly prepared hydrogen peroxide and guaiacum tincture.
3. Dissolve agar and gelatine completely before cooling.
4. Avoid lumps: sprinkle gums slowly into water with stirring.
5. Handle soda lime and acids carefully.

## Viva questions

1. **Give the biological source of acacia.** Dried gummy exudate from stems and branches of *Acacia senegal*; Leguminosae.
2. **Which enzyme in acacia gives the guaiacum test?** Oxidase (with peroxidase).
3. **Why must acacia be heated before use in some emulsions with easily oxidised drugs?** To destroy its oxidase enzyme.
4. **Name the two parts of tragacanth.** Tragacanthin (soluble) and bassorin (swells).
5. **How is agar told from gelatine?** Agar gives no precipitate with tannic acid and is Molisch-positive; gelatine gives a buff precipitate and is biuret-positive.
6. **Give the chemical nature of guar gum.** Galactomannan.
7. **Name the two types of gelatine.** Type A (acid-treated) and Type B (alkali-treated).
8. **Which reagent stains mucilage pink?** Ruthenium red.
practicals.title: Physical and chemical tests: Acacia, Tragacanth, Agar, Guar gum and Gelatine

practicals.markdown:
# Physical and chemical tests: Asafoetida and Benzoin

**Aim:** To identify asafoetida (an oleo-gum-resin) and benzoin (a balsamic resin) by physical and chemical tests.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Work in a fume cupboard for heating and sublimation tests.

## Principle

- **Asafoetida** contains resin (ferulic acid esters), gum and a sulphur-containing volatile oil. Its gum forms an emulsion with water. On hydrolysis with HCl it gives **umbelliferone**, which shows a **blue fluorescence** in alkaline solution.
- **Benzoin** is a balsam containing free **benzoic acid** (and, in Sumatra benzoin, free **cinnamic acid**). Benzoic acid **sublimes** on heating. Cinnamic acid is oxidised by potassium permanganate to **benzaldehyde**, which has a bitter-almond odour.

## Requirements

Asafoetida, Sumatra and Siam benzoin; mortar and pestle; test tubes; dry test tube with a cooled watch glass or cotton plug for sublimation; filter paper; spirit lamp; water bath; reagents — conc. H2SO4, conc. HCl, dilute ammonia, alcohol (90%), 1% potassium permanganate, dilute H2SO4; UV lamp (365 nm).

## Procedure and observations

**A. Asafoetida**

| No. | Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Note colour, odour and taste (do not swallow) | Yellowish-brown to reddish tears or mass; strong, garlic-like, unpleasant odour; bitter acrid taste | Characteristic of asafoetida |
| 2 | Triturate 0.5 g with 5 ml water | Orange-yellow (milky) **emulsion** forms | Gum + resin present |
| 3 | Put a drop of conc. H2SO4 on a freshly broken surface | **Red to reddish-brown** colour | Asafoetida resin |
| 4 | Boil 0.5 g with 5 ml conc. HCl for about a minute, filter, dilute the filtrate with water, make alkaline with dilute ammonia, view under UV light | **Blue fluorescence** | Umbelliferone formed on hydrolysis |
| 5 | Shake 1 g with 10 ml alcohol and filter; pour filtrate into water | Milky turbidity | Resin present |

**B. Benzoin**

| No. | Test | Sumatra benzoin | Siam benzoin | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Appearance and odour | Greyish-brown masses of whitish tears in a reddish-brown matrix; odour like storax | Yellowish-brown tears, flattened; odour like vanilla | Two commercial types |
| 2 | Heat about 0.5 g in a dry test tube with a cool watch glass on top | White **crystalline sublimate** on the cool surface | White crystalline sublimate | **Benzoic acid** present |
| 3 | Warm 0.5 g with 10 ml 1% KMnO4 (slightly acidified) | **Odour of benzaldehyde** (bitter almond) | No benzaldehyde odour | **Cinnamic acid** present only in Sumatra benzoin |
| 4 | Dissolve 0.5 g in 5 ml alcohol, filter, pour into water | Milky emulsion | Milky emulsion | Resin present |

**Comparison table**

| Feature | Asafoetida | Benzoin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Oleo-gum-resin | Balsam (balsamic resin) |
| Source | *Ferula assa-foetida* (Umbelliferae) | *Styrax benzoin* / *S. tonkinensis* (Styracaceae) |
| Key test | Blue fluorescence (umbelliferone); emulsion with water | Sublimate of benzoic acid; KMnO4 test for cinnamic acid |

## Result

- The sample forming an emulsion with water, giving red with H2SO4 and blue fluorescence after HCl hydrolysis is **asafoetida**.
- The sample giving a sublimate of benzoic acid is **benzoin**; the one also giving benzaldehyde odour with KMnO4 is **Sumatra benzoin**, and the one without it is **Siam benzoin**.

## Precautions

1. Perform heating and sublimation in a fume cupboard; do not inhale fumes.
2. Use a perfectly dry test tube for sublimation.
3. Use a freshly broken surface of asafoetida for the H2SO4 test.
4. View fluorescence in a dark area under UV light; never look directly at the UV source.
5. Warm KMnO4 mixtures gently; do not boil over.

## Viva questions

1. **What is an oleo-gum-resin? Give two examples.** A resin with gum and volatile oil — asafoetida, myrrh (also guggul).
2. **Give the biological source of asafoetida.** Oleo-gum-resin from the rhizome and roots of *Ferula assa-foetida* and other *Ferula* species; Umbelliferae.
3. **Which compound causes the blue fluorescence in the asafoetida test?** Umbelliferone.
4. **Name common adulterants of asafoetida.** Gum arabic, rosin, gypsum, red clay, chalk, flour, stones.
5. **How do you differentiate Sumatra and Siam benzoin?** Sumatra contains cinnamic acid and gives benzaldehyde odour with KMnO4; Siam does not.
6. **What is Friar's balsam?** Compound benzoin tincture, used as an inhalation in cough and as a skin protective.
7. **Why is benzoin called a balsam?** It contains benzoic and/or cinnamic acid and their esters.
8. **What gives asafoetida its smell?** Sulphur compounds (disulphides) of its volatile oil.
practicals.title: Physical and chemical tests: Asafoetida and Benzoin

practicals.markdown:
# Physical and chemical tests: Pale catechu and Black catechu

**Aim:** To identify pale catechu (gambir) and black catechu (kattha) by physical and chemical tests and to distinguish between them.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ.

## Principle

Both catechus are dried aqueous extracts rich in **condensed tannins and catechins**. They therefore give tannin tests (greenish-black with ferric chloride, precipitate with gelatin) and the **matchstick test**: catechins heated with HCl give phloroglucinol-type products that colour the lignin of the matchstick wood pink to red.

Pale catechu also contains **gambir-fluorescein**, which gives a **green fluorescence** in petroleum ether after treatment with alkali. Black catechu does not.

## Requirements

Samples of pale catechu and black catechu; test tubes; beakers; filter paper; matchsticks (wooden, unburnt end); spirit lamp; separating funnel or test tube; reagents — 5% ferric chloride, 1% gelatin solution with 10% sodium chloride, conc. HCl, alcohol, sodium hydroxide solution, petroleum ether, vanillin in HCl (vanillin–HCl reagent), lead acetate solution.

## Procedure

Prepare an extract of each sample: boil 1 g with 20 ml water, cool and filter (aqueous extract). Also prepare an alcoholic extract by warming 0.5 g with 10 ml alcohol and filtering.

## Observations

| No. | Test | Pale catechu | Black catechu | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Appearance | Pale brown to dull reddish-brown **cubes**, porous, friable | **Dark brown to black** irregular pieces, glossy fracture | Two types of catechu |
| 2 | Odour and taste | Odourless; bitter, astringent, then sweetish | Odourless; astringent, then sweetish | Tannin drugs |
| 3 | Aqueous extract + 5% FeCl3 | Greenish-black | Greenish-black | **Condensed tannins** |
| 4 | Aqueous extract + gelatin–NaCl solution | White/buff precipitate | White/buff precipitate | Tannins present (protein precipitated) |
| 5 | Aqueous extract + lead acetate | Precipitate | Precipitate | Tannins / phenolics |
| 6 | **Matchstick test**: dip the wooden end of a matchstick in the extract, dry it, moisten with conc. HCl, warm near (not in) the flame | Pink to red | Pink to red | **Catechins** present |
| 7 | Vanillin–HCl reagent on the extract | Pink to red | Pink to red | Catechins (flavan-3-ols) |
| 8 | **Gambir-fluorescein test**: alcoholic extract + a few drops NaOH, add petroleum ether, shake, allow layers to separate | **Green fluorescence** in the petroleum ether layer | No green fluorescence | Distinguishes **pale catechu** |

**Comparison**

| Feature | Pale catechu | Black catechu |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | Extract of leaves and young shoots of *Uncaria gambier* | Extract of heartwood of *Acacia catechu* |
| Family | Rubiaceae | Leguminosae |
| Form | Pale brown cubes | Dark brown to black masses |
| Gambir-fluorescein | Positive | Negative |

## Result

Both samples gave positive tests for condensed tannins and catechins. The sample giving a green fluorescence in the gambir-fluorescein test was identified as **pale catechu**; the dark sample that did not was identified as **black catechu**.

## Precautions

1. Use the unburnt wooden end of the matchstick and warm it gently; do not let it catch fire.
2. Use freshly prepared ferric chloride and gelatin solutions.
3. Let the petroleum ether layer separate fully before observing fluorescence; keep petroleum ether away from flames.
4. Filter extracts so that turbidity is not mistaken for a precipitate.

## Viva questions

1. **Give the biological source of pale catechu.** Dried aqueous extract of the leaves and young shoots of *Uncaria gambier*; Rubiaceae.
2. **Give the biological source of black catechu.** Dried aqueous extract of the heartwood of *Acacia catechu*; Leguminosae.
3. **What does the matchstick test show?** The presence of catechins; the matchstick wood turns pink-red after HCl and warming.
4. **Why does catechu give a greenish-black colour with FeCl3?** It contains condensed (catechol-type) tannins.
5. **Which test distinguishes pale from black catechu?** Gambir-fluorescein test — green fluorescence for pale catechu only.
6. **Give two uses of catechu.** Astringent in diarrhoea; gargles for sore throat and bleeding gums (also tanning and dyeing).
7. **What is the gelatin test?** Tannins precipitate gelatin (protein) from its solution.
8. **To which class of tannins do catechus belong?** Condensed tannins (phlobatannins).
practicals.title: Physical and chemical tests: Pale catechu and Black catechu

practicals.markdown:
# Physical and chemical tests: Castor oil

**Aim:** To identify castor oil by physical and chemical tests and to determine its acid value.

> Quantities are typical for a student batch. Follow your lab manual and your teacher where they differ. Wear goggles; keep solvents away from flames.

## Principle

Castor oil is the fixed oil expressed from the seeds of *Ricinus communis* (Euphorbiaceae). It consists mainly of triglycerides of **ricinoleic acid**, a hydroxy fatty acid. The hydroxyl group makes castor oil unusual among fixed oils:

- It is **very viscous**.
- It is **miscible with alcohol** (most fixed oils are not) and only **slightly soluble in light petroleum** (most fixed oils dissolve freely).

Like all fixed oils, it leaves a permanent grease spot, is saponified by alkali, and stains red with Sudan III.

**Acid value** is the number of mg of KOH needed to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of oil. A high value shows rancidity or poor quality.

## Requirements

Castor oil, another fixed oil for comparison (e.g. groundnut oil), filter paper, test tubes, measuring cylinders, Sudan III solution, alcohol (95%), light petroleum (petroleum ether), alcoholic KOH, water bath; for acid value — ethanol–ether (1 : 1) neutralised to phenolphthalein, 0.1 N KOH, phenolphthalein, conical flask, burette, balance.

## Procedure and observations

**A. Identification tests**

| No. | Test | Observation | Inference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Appearance and odour | Pale yellow or nearly colourless, thick, viscous liquid; slight odour; taste bland then slightly acrid | Castor oil characters |
| 2 | Viscosity: tilt a test tube of castor oil and of groundnut oil side by side | Castor oil flows much more slowly | High viscosity |
| 3 | Spot test: a drop on filter paper, leave for some time | Permanent translucent spot | Fixed oil |
| 4 | Oil + Sudan III, shake | Oil layer stained red | Fixed oil |
| 5 | Mix 1 ml oil with 1 ml alcohol (95%) | Clear, uniform solution | Castor oil (miscible with alcohol) |
| 6 | Mix 1 ml oil with 5 ml light petroleum | Turbid; oil not fully dissolved | Castor oil (slightly soluble in light petroleum) |
| 7 | Comparison: repeat tests 5 and 6 with groundnut oil | Turbid in alcohol, clear in light petroleum | Ordinary fixed oil behaves the opposite way |
| 8 | Saponification: warm 1 ml oil with 5 ml alcoholic KOH on a water bath; add water | Clear soapy solution; froths on shaking | Ester (glyceride) saponified |

**B. Acid value**

1. Weigh about 5 g of oil (W) accurately into a conical flask.
2. Add 50 ml of the neutralised ethanol–ether mixture; shake to dissolve.
3. Add a few drops of phenolphthalein; titrate with 0.1 N KOH until a faint pink colour persists for 30 seconds.
4. Note the volume used (V ml); repeat to get concordant readings.

**Formula**

Acid value = (56.1 × N × V) ÷ W

where N = normality of KOH, V = ml of KOH, W = weight of oil in g, 56.1 = molecular weight of KOH.

**Worked example (specimen readings)**

| Trial | Weight of oil (g) | Burette initial (ml) | Burette final (ml) | Volume used (ml) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 5.02 | 0.0 | 1.2 | 1.2 |
| 2 | 5.00 | 1.2 | 2.4 | 1.2 |

Acid value = (56.1 × 0.1 × 1.2) ÷ 5.0 = 6.73 ÷ 5.0 ≈ **1.35 mg KOH/g**

Compare your result with the pharmacopoeial limit given in your lab manual (a low value indicates good-quality, fresh oil).

## Result

The sample was identified as **castor oil** (viscous, miscible with alcohol, slightly soluble in light petroleum, permanent spot, saponifiable). Its acid value was found to be ___ mg KOH/g.

## Precautions

1. Neutralise the ethanol–ether before use so only free acids of the oil consume alkali.
2. Keep ether and light petroleum away from flames; warm only on a water bath.
3. Use clean, dry glassware for the solubility tests (water causes turbidity).
4. Titrate slowly near the end point and shake well.

## Viva questions

1. **Give the biological source of castor oil.** Fixed oil obtained by cold expression of the seeds of *Ricinus communis*; Euphorbiaceae.
2. **What is the chief fatty acid of castor oil?** Ricinoleic acid (a hydroxy fatty acid), about 80–90%.
3. **Why is castor oil soluble in alcohol?** The hydroxyl group of ricinoleic acid makes the oil more polar.
4. **How does castor oil act as a purgative?** Intestinal lipase releases ricinoleic acid, which irritates the intestine and increases movement.
5. **Why is castor oil cold-pressed?** To keep the toxic protein ricin (and ricinine) in the press-cake and out of the oil; heat also lowers quality.
6. **Define acid value.** Mg of KOH required to neutralise the free fatty acids in 1 g of fat or oil.
7. **Why does acid value rise on storage?** Moisture or lipase hydrolyses glycerides to free fatty acids (rancidity).
8. **Give two non-medicinal uses of castor oil.** Lubricant and plasticiser (also in soaps, paints and hair oils).
practicals.title: Physical and chemical tests: Castor oil

questions.answer:
1. Definition: pharmakon (drug) + gnosis (knowledge); study of crude drugs of plant, animal and mineral origin — identification, cultivation, collection, constituents, evaluation, preservation and uses. Term used by Schmidt (1811) and Seydler (1815, Analectica Pharmacognostica).
2. History: Vedas, Charaka Samhita (medicine) and Sushruta Samhita (surgery) in India; Shen Nung's herbal in China; Ebers papyrus (Egypt, about 1550 BC); Hippocrates (father of medicine), Theophrastus (father of botany), Dioscorides (De Materia Medica, about 600 plants), Galen (galenicals); Avicenna (Canon of Medicine); 19th century isolation of morphine and quinine; penicillin 1928; reserpine, vinca alkaloids, artemisinin.
3. Present status: WHO notes wide dependence on traditional medicine; many modern drugs are plant-derived (digoxin, morphine, quinine, reserpine, vincristine, taxol, artemisinin); AYUSH ministry and herbal industry; quality problems (adulteration, heavy metals); modern tools (HPTLC, HPLC, DNA barcoding); conservation of over-collected plants.
4. Scope: identification of crude drugs, detection of adulteration, standardisation, discovery of new drugs, semi-synthesis starting materials, pharmaceutical aids, herbal formulations, nutraceuticals and cosmetics, cultivation and biotechnology, export.
questions.question: Define pharmacognosy. Describe its history and the present status and scope of pharmacognosy.

questions.answer: Identification of genuine crude drugs; detection of adulteration; standardisation and quality control (ash, extractive, assay); source of new drugs (vincristine, artemisinin); starting materials for semi-synthesis (diosgenin → steroids, podophyllotoxin → etoposide); pharmaceutical aids (acacia, tragacanth, beeswax); herbal formulations, nutraceuticals and cosmetics; cultivation, tissue culture and conservation; scientific study of traditional systems; export of herbal products.
questions.question: Write a short note on the scope of pharmacognosy.

questions.answer: Hippocrates — father of medicine; treated disease as a natural process and used herbs. Dioscorides — Greek physician, wrote De Materia Medica (1st century AD) describing about 600 plants; used for over 1,500 years. Galen — prepared extracts and mixtures of plant drugs; such preparations are called galenicals. Avicenna (Ibn Sina) — wrote the Canon of Medicine, the basis of the Unani system.
questions.question: Write the contribution of Hippocrates, Dioscorides, Galen and Avicenna to pharmacognosy.

questions.answer: Herbal medicine is widely used worldwide and in India under AYUSH. Many modern drugs come from plants: digoxin (Digitalis lanata, heart failure), morphine and codeine (opium), quinine (cinchona, malaria), reserpine (rauwolfia, hypertension), vincristine and vinblastine (Catharanthus, cancer), paclitaxel (Taxus, cancer), artemisinin (Artemisia annua, malaria), ephedrine (ephedra, asthma). Current focus: standardisation, safety, modern analytical methods and conservation.
questions.question: Give the present status of pharmacognosy with examples of plant-derived modern drugs.

questions.answer: Rigveda and Atharvaveda mention medicinal plants; Atharvaveda is the root of Ayurveda. Charaka Samhita covers internal medicine with hundreds of plant drugs. Sushruta Samhita covers surgery (Sushruta: father of Indian surgery). Vagbhata wrote Ashtanga Hridaya. Long-used Indian plants: turmeric, neem, tulsi, ginger, black pepper, rauwolfia, ashwagandha.
questions.question: Write a note on the history of pharmacognosy in ancient India.

questions.answer: Pharmacognosy is the study of crude drugs of natural (plant, animal, mineral) origin — their identification, constituents, evaluation, preservation and uses. From Greek pharmakon (drug) and gnosis (knowledge).
questions.question: Define pharmacognosy.

questions.answer: J. A. Schmidt used it in 1811, and C. A. Seydler used it as the title of his work Analectica Pharmacognostica in 1815.
questions.question: Who coined the term pharmacognosy?

questions.answer: A natural substance of plant, animal or mineral origin that has only been collected and dried, not further processed. Examples: senna leaves, cinchona bark.
questions.question: What is a crude drug? Give two examples.

questions.answer: Preparations such as tinctures and extracts made by extracting or mixing crude drugs, named after the Greek physician Galen.
questions.question: What are galenicals?

questions.answer: An ancient Egyptian medical scroll (about 1550 BC) listing many remedies made from drugs such as aloe, castor oil, opium and myrrh.
questions.question: What is the Ebers papyrus?

questions.answer:
1. Alphabetical — drugs in A–Z order of Latin or English names; used in IP, BP, USP. Merits: quick reference, easy to add drugs. Demerits: no link between drugs, no information on source or action.
2. Taxonomical — by kingdom, order, family, genus (Solanaceae: belladonna, datura; Rubiaceae: cinchona, ipecac). Merits: shows natural relationship. Demerits: drugs with different actions together; changes in taxonomy.
3. Morphological — by part used: organised (leaves: senna; barks: cinnamon; roots: rauwolfia; seeds: nutmeg) and unorganised (gums: acacia; resins: benzoin; latex: opium; oils: castor oil). Merits: helps identification. Demerits: ignores chemistry and action.
4. Pharmacological — by action (laxatives: senna; cardiotonics: digitalis; carminatives: clove). Merits: most useful to pharmacists. Demerits: one drug may have many actions.
5. Chemical — by main constituent (alkaloids: cinchona; glycosides: senna; tannins: catechu; volatile oils: clove). Merits: helps assay and research. Demerits: drugs with several groups.
6. Chemo-taxonomical — related plants contain related chemicals (tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae). Merits: helps classification and new drug search. Demerits: exceptions (caffeine in unrelated plants), needs analysis.
questions.question: Classify crude drugs. Explain the different systems of classification with examples, merits and demerits.

questions.answer: Basis: part of plant or animal used. Organised drugs (cellular): leaves — senna, digitalis; flower buds — clove; fruits — coriander, fennel; seeds — ispaghula, nutmeg; barks — cinnamon, cinchona; roots — rauwolfia, ipecac; rhizomes — ginger, turmeric; herbs — vinca; sclerotium — ergot. Unorganised drugs (non-cellular): latex — opium; dried juice — aloe; extracts — catechu, agar; gums — acacia, tragacanth; resins and balsams — benzoin, tolu; oleo-gum-resins — asafoetida; oils — castor oil; waxes — beeswax. Merit: identification. Demerit: no information on chemistry or action.
questions.question: Write a note on morphological classification of crude drugs with examples.

questions.answer: Basis: main active chemical. Alkaloids — cinchona, opium, rauwolfia; anthraquinone glycosides — senna, aloe; cardiac glycosides — digitalis, squill; saponins — liquorice; tannins — catechu, myrobalan, galls; volatile oils — clove, cinnamon, fennel; resins — benzoin, tolu; carbohydrates — acacia, agar; lipids — castor oil, beeswax; enzymes — papain, pancreatin. Merits: explains action, helps chemical evaluation and research. Demerits: drugs containing more than one group are difficult to place; structures of some actives unknown.
questions.question: Explain chemical classification of crude drugs with merits and demerits.

questions.answer: Classification that uses chemical constituents together with taxonomy, based on the idea that related plants make related compounds (chemosystematics). Examples: tropane alkaloids in Solanaceae (belladonna, datura, hyoscyamus); indole alkaloids in Apocynaceae (rauwolfia, vinca); cardiac glycosides in Scrophulariaceae and Apocynaceae; volatile oil in vittae in Umbelliferae. Merits: settles doubtful plant positions, guides new drug search. Demerit: exceptions such as caffeine in unrelated plants.
questions.question: What is chemo-taxonomical classification? Give examples.

questions.answer: Pharmacological: based on therapeutic action (laxatives — senna, aloe; cardiotonics — digitalis; antimalarials — cinchona). Most useful to pharmacists; but one drug may have several actions. Taxonomical: based on botanical family, genus and species (Solanaceae — belladonna, ashwagandha; Zingiberaceae — ginger, turmeric). Shows natural relationship; but drugs with very different actions fall together and plant classification keeps changing.
questions.question: Compare pharmacological and taxonomical classification of drugs.

questions.answer: Organised drugs have a cellular structure and are direct plant/animal parts (senna leaf). Unorganised drugs are non-cellular products such as gums, resins, latex and oils (acacia, opium).
questions.question: What are organised and unorganised drugs? Give one example each.

questions.answer: The alphabetical system (drugs arranged A to Z by name).
questions.question: Which system of classification is followed in pharmacopoeias?

questions.answer: It shows no relationship between drugs, and gives no information about source, part used, constituents or action.
questions.question: Give two demerits of alphabetical classification.

questions.answer: Family Zingiberaceae; order Zingiberales (Scitamineae).
questions.question: Name the family of ginger and write its order.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: substituting the genuine drug fully or partly with inferior, cheaper, exhausted, harmful or useless material, or mixing such material with it; deliberate or accidental.
2. Reasons: high price, scarcity, similar appearance, confusion of names, careless collection, poor storage.
3. Methods:
(a) Inferior commercial varieties — Cassia auriculata for senna; Amomum for cardamom; cassia bark for cinnamon.
(b) Artificially manufactured substitutes — paraffin wax coloured as beeswax; artificial invert sugar for honey.
(c) Exhausted drugs — exhausted ginger and clove.
(d) Superficially similar cheaper material — papaya seeds in black pepper.
(e) Worthless heavy material — stones in asafoetida, sand and lead in opium.
(f) Synthetic principles — citral added to lemon oil, benzyl benzoate to balsams.
(g) Vegetative parts of the same plant — clove stalks, senna stems.
(h) Harmful adulterants — metanil yellow or lead chromate in turmeric.
(i) Deteriorated, mouldy or insect-damaged drugs.
4. Sophistication: skilful deliberate adulteration, especially of powders.
questions.question: Define adulteration. Describe the different methods of adulteration of crude drugs with suitable examples.

questions.answer:
1. Evaluation = confirming identity and determining quality and purity; needed because of natural variation, effect of drying/storage and adulteration.
2. Morphological (organoleptic): colour, odour, taste, size, shape, surface, fracture (aromatic clove, bitter cinchona, quills of cinnamon).
3. Microscopical: TS, powder characters (trichomes, stomata, fibres, stone cells, crystals, starch); staining (phloroglucinol–HCl for lignin, iodine for starch); quantitative — stomatal number, stomatal index S/(S+E)×100, palisade ratio, vein-islet and vein termination number; micrometry; lycopodium spore method.
4. Physical: moisture content, ash values (total, acid-insoluble, water-soluble, sulphated), extractive values (alcohol, water, ether), volatile oil content, swelling factor, viscosity, melting point, refractive index, optical rotation, foaming index, UV fluorescence.
5. Chemical: identification tests (Borntrager's, Keller–Killiani, murexide), assays of active constituents, chemical constants (acid, saponification, iodine values), chromatography.
6. Biological: bioassay when chemical assay is not possible — digitalis on pigeon/frog, ergot; also microbial counts, aflatoxins, pesticides, heavy metals.
questions.question: What is evaluation of crude drugs? Describe the various methods of evaluation.

questions.answer: Ash values: residue after incinerating the drug at about 450 °C. Total ash — all inorganic matter. Acid-insoluble ash — residue after boiling total ash with dilute HCl; shows sand and earth. Water-soluble ash — water-soluble part of total ash; helps detect exhausted drugs. Sulphated ash — drug treated with H2SO4 before ignition. Extractive values: percentage of drug soluble in a solvent — alcohol-soluble (resins, alkaloids, glycosides), water-soluble (tannins, sugars, mucilage), ether-soluble (oils). Low values suggest exhausted or adulterated drug.
questions.question: Write a note on ash values and extractive values.

questions.answer: Stomatal number — average number of stomata per sq. mm of epidermis. Stomatal index — SI = S ÷ (S + E) × 100, S stomata and E epidermal cells in the same area; fairly constant for a species. Palisade ratio — average number of palisade cells under one epidermal cell. Vein-islet number — number of vein islets per sq. mm. Vein termination number — vein endings per sq. mm. Used to distinguish related species such as Indian and Alexandrian senna. Also micrometry and lycopodium spore method.
questions.question: Write a note on quantitative microscopy (leaf constants).

questions.answer: Used to find the percentage of a genuine drug in a powder. Lycopodium spores are very uniform in size and number (about 94,000 per mg). A known weight of the sample is mixed with a known weight of lycopodium; the mixture is mounted and the characteristic particles of the drug (e.g. starch grains, cells) and the spores are counted in several fields. From the ratio and the known number of spores, the amount of genuine drug is calculated. Useful for powdered drugs.
questions.question: Explain the lycopodium spore method.

questions.answer: Uses sense organs — colour (pale green senna, reddish-brown cinchona), odour (aromatic clove, garlic-like asafoetida), taste (bitter aloe, pungent ginger, sweet liquorice), size and shape (nail-shaped clove 10–17.5 mm), surface and fracture (fibrous cinchona, short rauwolfia), special features (quills of cinnamon, asymmetric senna base). Quick, cheap, first step of identification and detects gross adulteration.
questions.question: Write the importance of organoleptic evaluation with examples.

questions.answer: Percentage of stomata out of the total number of epidermal cells and stomata in a unit area. SI = S ÷ (S + E) × 100.
questions.question: Define stomatal index and give its formula.

questions.answer: Dried papaya seeds (Carica papaya).
questions.question: Name the adulterant of black pepper.

questions.answer: The amount of silica, sand and earthy matter, i.e. soil contamination of the drug.
questions.question: What does acid-insoluble ash indicate?

questions.answer: Digitalis and ergot.
questions.question: Name two drugs evaluated by bioassay.

questions.answer: A deliberate and skilful form of adulteration in which an imitation is made to closely resemble the genuine drug, mostly in powders.
questions.question: What is sophistication?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: basic, nitrogen-containing organic compounds of plant origin, usually with N in a heterocyclic ring, with marked physiological action; mostly bitter, crystalline; free bases soluble in organic solvents, salts in water.
2. Occurrence: mostly dicots (Solanaceae, Papaveraceae, Apocynaceae, Rubiaceae, Leguminosae); in leaves, bark, roots, seeds, latex; as salts of plant acids (meconic, quinic).
